payload.task_text:
I need to build a comprehensive research knowledge base for our team studying large language models. Start by searching for recent scholarly papers on topics like "large language models", "prompt engineering", and "in-context learning". Find at least 5 relevant papers.

Then use the paper repository to download and read the full content of the most relevant papers. Analyze their LaTeX source when available to extract detailed methodology sections.

Write and run a Python script called research_synthesizer.py in the workspace that reads papers_metadata.json and papers_contents.json (create both first), extracts key methods, creates a citation network map, calculates relevance scores, and outputs research_synthesis.json.

Create an Excel file called Research_Knowledge_Base.xlsx with three sheets. The first sheet Paper_Catalog should have columns Paper_ID, Title, Authors, Year, Category, and Citation_Count, sorted by Citation_Count descending. The second sheet Method_Comparison should have columns Method_Name, Paper_Source, Key_Innovation, Benchmark_Result, and Applicability ("High", "Medium", "Low"). The third sheet Research_Gaps should have Gap_Area, Current_State, Opportunity, and Priority ("Critical", "Important", "Nice-to-have") columns with at least 4 identified gaps. In the Excel file, write all values as literal text/numbers directly into the cells; do not use Excel formulas.

Create a Notion page titled "LLM Research Hub" with a heading "Large Language Model Research Dashboard". Add paragraphs covering research landscape overview, key papers summary, methodology comparison highlights, and identified research gaps with recommendations for future work.

Task-Solving Rationable with Sub-task Decomposition:
To solve this task efficiently, use exactly one paper-processing wave. The main agent first reads all task-visible guide and team-interest files, then issues bounded native-parallel searches for the three literal topics `large language models`, `prompt engineering`, and `in-context learning` in both Scholarly and local arXiv. Union by stable ID, reject off-topic results by title/abstract, and freeze exactly five strongest papers covering all three topics in a literal dispatch table `{agent_no, paper_id, title, citation_count, category}`.

1. Wave 1 — dispatch exactly 5 explore sub-agents through one same-template AgentSwarm call:

   1. explore 0 (academic-literature-researcher 0): Explore 0 owns only dispatch-table row 1 and its literal paper ID.
   2. explore 1 (academic-literature-researcher 1): Explore 1 owns only dispatch-table row 2 and its literal paper ID.
   3. explore 2 (academic-literature-researcher 2): Explore 2 owns only dispatch-table row 3 and its literal paper ID.
   4. explore 3 (academic-literature-researcher 3): Explore 3 owns only dispatch-table row 4 and its literal paper ID.
   5. explore 4 (academic-literature-researcher 4): Explore 4 owns only dispatch-table row 5 and its literal paper ID.

For its one row, each explore sub-agent retrieves/downloads and reads the full local paper, inspects available arXiv-LaTeX sections, and writes one unique `paper_<safe_id>.json` containing exact metadata, authors, year, citation count, category, abstract, full-content/method evidence, benchmark evidence, and source-supported references. Return only its path, ID, schema/count controls, and read status. Do not write any required final filename or modify Notion.

After Wave 1, the main agent checks the five paths and IDs once, consolidates them into `papers_metadata.json` and `papers_contents.json`, writes and runs `research_synthesizer.py` exactly once, and verifies `research_synthesis.json`. It then creates `Research_Knowledge_Base.xlsx` and the single `LLM Research Hub` page as independent native-parallel output branches from that verified synthesis. The workbook must use exactly `Paper_Catalog`, `Method_Comparison`, and `Research_Gaps`, literal values, citation-descending catalog rows, controlled applicability labels, and at least four evidence-backed gaps. The page must contain the exact dashboard heading and the four requested substantive sections. Read each final output once and do not dispatch another wave.

Create a Notion page that serves as the research dashboard hub for a team studying large language models. You have Notion API tools (mcp__notion__API-post-page, mcp__notion__API-post-search, mcp__notion__API-retrieve-a-page, etc.).

PAGE PLACEMENT: Create the page at the workspace root, i.e. use parent {"type": "workspace", "workspace": true}. (An existing page "Meeting Notes Archive" is parented at the workspace root, confirming root-level creation is possible — do NOT use it as parent and do NOT modify or comment on it.)

PAGE TITLE (page name property): "LLM Research Hub" — set via the title property, e.g. properties: {"title": {"title": [{"text": {"content": "LLM Research Hub"}}]}} (if the "title" property name is rejected, try "Title" or "Name").

PAGE CONTENT — the page must start with a heading_1 block with the exact text: "Large Language Model Research Dashboard". Then add the sections below. Use heading_2 blocks for the four section titles and paragraph blocks for the body text (keep the text verbatim; do not shorten). Structure:

[heading_1] Large Language Model Research Dashboard

[heading_2] Research Landscape Overview
[paragraph] This hub consolidates the team's knowledge base on large language models. Five scholarly papers were retrieved from the arXiv paper repository against three research topics - large language models, prompt engineering, and in-context learning - and were analyzed by the research_synthesizer.py pipeline (relevance scoring, citation-network mapping, and research-gap prioritization). The corpus spans January-May 2023 and consists of two surveys (LLM Reasoning Survey; Survey of In-Context Learning for Large Language Models), one practitioner guide (Prompt Engineering Guide), one empirical study (Chain-of-Thought Reasoning in Large Language Models), and one theoretical work (In-Context Learning Theory).
[paragraph] The inferred citation network is densely connected: 9 of 10 possible links exist (density 0.9), because the papers share key methods, arXiv categories and topic tags. The LLM Reasoning Survey (2301.00001) is the most connected node (weighted degree 10.5) and acts as the corpus hub, while the strongest single link connects the Reasoning Survey to the Chain-of-Thought study (2304.00004) through their shared chain-of-thought method. The repository exposes no reference lists and no citation counts, so network links are inferred from shared methods, categories and topic tags, and the citation counts used for ranking are model-based estimates (relevance x publication age x category breadth) as of 2026-09-02.

[heading_2] Key Papers Summary
[paragraph] The most relevant paper is Chain-of-Thought Reasoning in Large Language Models (2304.00004, Author F, 2023, relevance 100/100, ~205 estimated citations), which studies chain-of-thought prompting strategies for LLMs. The Survey of In-Context Learning for Large Language Models (2305.00005, Author G, relevance 96.3, ~160 estimated citations) aggregates in-context learning approaches. The LLM Reasoning Survey (2301.00001, Author A, relevance 74.1, ~163) organizes reasoning methods into a comparative taxonomy. In-Context Learning Theory (2303.00003, Author C, relevance 48.1, ~84) provides the formal foundations of in-context learning, and the Prompt Engineering Guide (2302.00002, Author B, relevance 44.4, ~80) distills practical prompt design patterns. Full-text bodies were empty in the repository, and LaTeX source was available only for 2301.00001 and 2302.00002 (title-level skeletons with no methodology sections), so the analysis leans on abstracts and curated reading notes.

[heading_2] Methodology Comparison Highlights
[paragraph] Six method families were extracted across the corpus. Chain-of-Thought prompting (primary source 2304.00004; echoed in 2301.00001 and 2302.00002) is the most mature: eliciting intermediate reasoning steps via few-shot exemplars delivers large gains on multi-step arithmetic and reasoning benchmarks (GSM8K-class tasks) - applicability High. Structured Prompt Design (2302.00002) and In-Context Learning (2305.00005, 2303.00003) are also rated High applicability: the former covers instruction formatting, exemplar selection and prompt composition without weight updates, while the latter is task acquisition directly from demonstrations with no fine-tuning, with few-shot gains that grow with model scale. Demonstration Selection and Ordering Strategies (2305.00005, 2302.00002) and the Reasoning Method Taxonomy (2301.00001) are rated Medium: surveyed evidence shows demonstration choice and ordering can swing task accuracy substantially, but neither offers isolated experimental comparisons. The Theoretical Analysis of In-Context Learning (2303.00003) is rated Low direct applicability because its formal results on idealized settings are not yet empirically validated at production scale.

[heading_2] Identified Research Gaps and Recommendations for Future Work
[paragraph] Eight gaps were prioritized by severity x (1 - corpus coverage), aligned with the team's stated interests. Critical: (1) Hallucination mitigation in reasoning chains - no corpus paper addresses error propagation or confidence calibration in generated reasoning chains; recommended future work: verification and self-correction layers over chain-of-thought outputs with per-step calibrated confidence. (2) Standardized benchmarking of prompting strategies - prompt engineering guidance is qualitative and surveys aggregate incompatible protocols; recommended future work: a reproducible benchmark suite across reasoning and instruction-following tasks to quantify which prompt patterns generalize across models.
[paragraph] Important: (3) In-context learning vs. parameter-efficient fine-tuning - run head-to-head adaptation studies reporting quality, data cost and compute cost. (4) Multilingual and cross-lingual evaluation - extend prompting and ICL studies beyond English-centric settings. (5) Theory-practice bridge for in-context learning - empirically test the formal predictions of 2303.00003 on production-scale models. (6) Robustness and safety of in-context learning - audit sensitivity to demonstration ordering and poisoned exemplars. (7) Efficiency and cost of prompting strategies - develop cost-aware prompting that selects reasoning depth and demonstration count per query. Nice-to-have: (8) Unified evaluation and reproducibility infrastructure - a shared evaluation harness and common taxonomy for cross-paper comparison. Recommended sequence: start with the two Critical gaps, since standardized benchmarking unblocks measurable progress on every other item, and hallucination control is the precondition for deploying prompted reasoning in production.
[paragraph] Supporting artifacts live in the team workspace: papers_metadata.json, papers_contents.json, research_synthesizer.py, research_synthesis.json, and Research_Knowledge_Base.xlsx (sheets: Paper_Catalog, Method_Comparison, Research_Gaps).

NOTES:
- Create the page once (do not create duplicates). If a page titled "LLM Research Hub" already exists from your earlier work, reuse/update it instead of creating a second one.
- All blocks are simple: heading_1, heading_2, and paragraph rich-text blocks. No databases, no comments, no other writes.

DELIVERABLE: report the created page's ID and title, the parent used, the number and types of blocks created, and confirmation that the page is not archived. If the workspace-root parent is rejected, fall back to searching for an accessible parent page (but do not use "Meeting Notes Archive") and report which parent you used.
